\calmregularHoloBoxing: A Simple Recipe for Humanoid Boxing with 7 Minutes of Single-GPU Training

\calmregularXihan Ma Equal contribution.    \calmregularBo Zhang Equal contribution.    \calmregularBoxiong Li    \calmregularYuhan Bao    \calmregularZiyue Liu    \calmregularYucheng Wang
Abstract

HoloBoxing presents a simple recipe for learning humanoid boxing by building on a pretrained whole-body controller. The recipe separates reusable motor skills from task decisions: a compact planner requests future body-point targets, while the frozen controller handles joint-level execution. A learned decoder maps 32-dimensional actions to structured target windows, and measured-state imitation initializes the planner before reinforcement learning. Task learning then refines interaction behavior while reusing the decoder and controller, avoiding the need to relearn whole-body control. This combination keeps task optimization focused on a compact upper policy and supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven exploration. Starting from that available controller, the recipe accounts for about seven minutes of additional training, including reused representation fitting and a single-GPU task run. This excludes controller pretraining, data preparation, evaluation, and search. Simulated boxing experiments and component controls evaluate the resulting behavior and the roles of imitation initialization and the target representation.

††correspondence: Yucheng Wang††date: 23 October 2026

\calmregular1 \calmregularIntroduction

A motion controller can reproduce a punch without deciding when or where to use it. Humanoid boxing adds an opponent, changing contact, and the need to remain upright after an exchange. Learning all of these behaviors from joint commands couples motor execution with task decisions. HoloBoxing instead asks how far a simple, short training recipe can go when whole-body motor capability is already available.

Reusable whole-body controllers make task adaptation above existing motor capability a practical starting point. The recipe separates what must be learned for boxing from what can be reused. A pretrained HoloMotion v2 controller executes movement requests and remains frozen. A learned target decoder represents short windows of future body-point poses with a 32-dimensional action. A compact feedback planner selects these actions from measured robot state and opponent positions. Task learning therefore adapts movement requests while retaining the underlying execution capability.

We initialize this planner through measured-state imitation before refining it with reinforcement learning. The fixed controller first tracks reference motions to collect actual robot observations and future-target labels. Supervised learning turns those pairs into an initial feedback policy. Standing warmup and interaction against a fixed standing opponent then adjust behavior through rewards. The decoder and lower controller are reused throughout, as illustrated in Figure 1.

These choices make the training problem smaller in three concrete ways. Controller reuse removes joint-level motor learning from task adaptation. The target representation reduces the planner’s action dimension from 225 coordinates to 32 latent variables. Imitation supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven exploration. Together, they define the simple recipe whose training cost and resulting behavior we evaluate.

The primary recipe accounts for 7.0 minutes, combining a new single-RTX-4090 run with previously recorded target-representation fitting. A 21.4-minute long version provides a higher-budget comparison. Simulation experiments assess whether this short adaptation produces interactive boxing, while matched-budget controls remove imitation initialization or the target decoder. We also test observation choices and representation quality to explain the interfaces used by the recipe. Detailed timings and competitive outcomes appear in the experiments; assumptions and remaining validation needs are discussed separately.

\calmregular2 \calmregularBackground and motivation

Humanoid boxing combines motor execution with decisions about approaching, striking, and responding to an opponent. Our focus is the additional learning needed when a general-purpose controller already supplies whole-body movement. Three established ideas motivate a simple task-adaptation recipe.

Reuse motor capability.

Motion imitation learns physically simulated movement from reference trajectories (Peng et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2023). Recent humanoid systems extend this approach toward reusable whole-body control (Fu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a). A task policy can request movement while a fixed controller converts those requests and robot feedback into joint commands. HoloBoxing uses the released HoloMotion v2 controller in this role. The boxing planner therefore learns task decisions above existing motor capability, rather than relearning joint-level execution. This separation also defines the cost boundary: we measure new task training and exclude the inherited controller’s pretraining. The task-specific problem is consequently to choose useful movement requests in response to an opponent. This differs from acquiring a broad motor repertoire and motivates evaluating adaptation time separately from controller development.

Represent movement requests compactly.

Latent representations organize reusable movements and skills (Peng et al., 2022; Tessler et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023), including spherical representations for state-conditioned motor control (Tan et al., 2026). HoloBoxing learns a decoder from a normalized 32-dimensional action to 225 future body-point target coordinates. This gives the planner a compact action interface while retaining the same lower controller. The representation supplies target structure, while the controller supplies motor feedback. Since reconstruction quality alone does not establish physical executability, we evaluate both target error and tracking behavior. The decoder and controller play different roles: one structures future requests, while the other responds to the robot’s current physical state. Keeping these roles separate lets the task policy reuse both interfaces as learning progresses.

Initialize before learning interaction.

Imitation supplies an initial behavior, and reinforcement learning adjusts it through executed interaction. Sports and boxing systems combine motion knowledge with task objectives in several forms (Ren et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2026). Adapting frozen motor models also provides a reusable basis for new behaviors (Vainshtein et al., 2026; Park et al., 2026). HoloBoxing initializes its planner from measured robot observations collected during reference tracking, then refines it through standing warmup and interaction rewards. The decoder and whole-body controller remain frozen throughout task learning. Measured observations matter because the executing robot can deviate from the reference trajectory. Training the planner on these states connects its initial behavior to the feedback available during interaction. Reinforcement learning can then focus on adapting that behavior to task rewards.

Together, these choices confine task adaptation to a compact feedback planner with an initial behavior and a reusable execution interface. The experiments measure the training cost and boxing behavior of this combined recipe. Component controls examine its ingredients without assuming a separate causal speedup from each one.

\calmregular3 \calmregularHoloBoxing

The recipe learns task decisions above a fixed motor controller. It fits a target representation, initializes a feedback planner, and refines that planner through interaction while preserving whole-body execution. For masked observation M⁡(ot)M(o_{t}), the execution chain is

zt=𝒩⁡(fθ​(M⁡(ot))),gt=Dϕ​(zt),at=πHM​(ct,gt).z_{t}=\mathcal{N}(f_{\theta}(M(o_{t}))),\qquad g_{t}=D_{\phi}(z_{t}),\qquad a_{t}=\pi_{\mathrm{HM}}(c_{t},g_{t}). (1)

Here, 𝒩⁡(u)=u/‖u‖\mathcal{N}(u)=u/\|u\| uses a fixed fallback at zero. The planner fθf_{\theta} requests targets gtg_{t} through decoder DϕD_{\phi}; the frozen controller πHM\pi_{\mathrm{HM}} combines them with robot feedback ctc_{t}.

The planner has hidden widths 256 and 128 and predicts a 32-dimensional action. Its 1095-dimensional normalized input retains 63 current-self features and 15 opponent-position features; the remaining entries are masked to zero. Masking selects information without reducing the input-layer width. The decoder expands the action to 225 position and orientation coordinates for five body points at five future times. Thus, task learning operates through a small upper network and action interface while reusing motor execution.

\calmregular3.1 \calmregularCompress movement requests before task learning

The first stage fits an encoder EψE_{\psi} and decoder DϕD_{\phi} to reference target windows xx. Using training statistics (μx,σx)(\mu_{x},\sigma_{x}) and x~=(x−μx)⊘σx\tilde{x}=(x-\mu_{x})\oslash\sigma_{x}, it minimizes

x^\displaystyle\hat{x} =Dϕ​(𝒩⁡(Eψ​(x~))),\displaystyle=D_{\phi}(\mathcal{N}(E_{\psi}(\tilde{x}))), (2)
ℒprior\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}} =𝔼x​[1225​‖(x^−x)⊘σx‖22].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\frac{1}{225}\|(\hat{x}-x)\oslash\sigma_{x}\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (3)

The symbol ⊘\oslash denotes componentwise division. The decoder restores physical target statistics and projects orientation features into valid rotations. After validation selects a checkpoint, its weights and statistics remain fixed. Only the decoder enters the executed boxing policy; the encoder remains an offline fitting and diagnostic component. This replaces direct target prediction with a learned 32-dimensional action space.

\calmregular3.2 \calmregularInitialize feedback before reward-driven exploration

The frozen controller tracks reference motions to collect measured robot observations and future-target labels. The planner learns from these pairs through the frozen decoder:

ℒIL​(θ)=𝔼(o,x)​[ℓtarget​(Dϕ​(𝒩⁡(fθ​(M⁡(o)))),x)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(o,x)}[\ell_{\mathrm{target}}(D_{\phi}(\mathcal{N}(f_{\theta}(M(o)))),x)]. (4)

The target loss equally weights dimension-normalized position and orientation errors. Gradients pass through the decoder to update the planner, while decoder weights remain fixed. Reference windows use their source pelvis frame; collected labels use the measured robot’s current pelvis frame with a shared horizontal alignment. This expresses supervision in the feedback frame from which the controller must execute it. Future reference states supply labels rather than actor inputs. The selected planner weights and observation statistics initialize task learning, providing behavior before reward-driven exploration. Appendix B specifies coordinate alignment and the complete target loss.

\calmregular3.3 \calmregularRefine task decisions while retaining motor execution

Proximal policy optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) first runs 32 standing-warmup updates against a passive opponent. The resulting weights and observation statistics initialize 128 interaction updates with fresh optimization state. The primary recipe uses a fixed external standing actor as its opponent throughout. The same opponent and its original observation statistics are shared by both component removals. Its reward combines task shaping and adversarial motion style (Peng et al., 2021) with weights 0.8 and 0.2. Task terms guide approach, facing, contact, and balance; the match referee separately determines competitive outcomes.

The planner, value estimator, and style discriminator train during task learning. The target decoder and HoloMotion controller stay frozen. The value estimator predicts future reward, and the discriminator compares simulated motion with reference examples. Reinforcement learning therefore refines task decisions while retaining the target representation and motor capability.

\calmregular4 \calmregularEvaluating short task adaptation

The evaluation asks whether the reused hierarchy produces interactive boxing after the recorded short training procedure. It measures training time, competitive behavior, and the effects of removing task-policy components. These measurements address different parts of the recipe: time quantifies adaptation cost, while behavior tests what that budget achieves.

All evaluated policies share the packaged robot, actuator settings, arena, simulator, and referee. They retain different observation definitions, so the league is not an observation-controlled comparison of methods. A valid hand contact scores a point, while a sustained fall can end the bout with a knockout. We retain contacts and falls alongside match outcomes because an opponent can lose without receiving a scored punch. Every bout lasts at most sixty seconds.

A fixed ten-round league gives each policy the same opponent coverage, with randomized sides and recorded initial-state seeds. Elo summarizes outcomes within this frozen participant pool; component controls provide comparisons within the HoloBoxing recipe. Recorded states, actions, and referee events allow replay without rerunning simulation. Appendix D specifies scoring thresholds, the rating equation, and replay conditions.

\calmregular5 \calmregularExperiments: training cost and resulting behavior

\calmregular5.1 \calmregularA small task learner above a fixed controller

The selected HoloBoxing recipe uses the Unitree G1 and the frozen HoloMotion v2 controller (Horizon Robotics, 2026). The motion corpus combines paired InterHuman data (Liang et al., 2024) and released RoboStriker trajectories (RoboStriker Authors, 2026). The 14 original training motions total 212.88 seconds after retargeting; both participants and mirrored versions remain grouped within each split. Prior fitting uses 21148 training windows, 11074 validation windows, and a separate test population of 3246 windows. Measured-state imitation uses 2568 training examples from six InterHuman motions and 6448 validation examples from two different motions. Appendix A provides source counts and training settings.

The decoder predicts five future poses for the pelvis, both wrists, and both ankles, spanning 20–100 ms. The planner retains current robot state and opponent positions; time and score are unused. PPO uses 128 parallel environments and 24-step rollouts. Validation selects the reused prior. The primary recipe uses the last scheduled imitation and task-training checkpoints. Appendices A and B retain dimensions, network widths, and optimization settings.

\calmregular5.2 \calmregularWhere the seven minutes are spent

Table 1 accounts for 422.2 seconds, or 7.0 minutes. The new process takes 375.0 seconds; previously recorded prior fitting adds 47.2 seconds. The headline therefore describes accounted training cost, rather than a fresh uninterrupted run of every stage on one machine. Representation fitting and imitation together account for 53.9 seconds; standing and interaction account for 360.2 seconds. The task learner reuses the lower controller throughout.

The total excludes controller pretraining, downloading, retargeting, observation collection, evaluation, and hyperparameter search. The fixed training opponent is also reused; its original training is outside this accounting. The total measures the primary learner and target-representation fitting above these available components. The primary version uses 128 interaction updates; the 21.4-minute long version uses 256 and a different recorded training path.

\calmregular5.3 \calmregularAdditional training above reusable motor capability

The relevant cost is the additional training needed once motor control is available. General-purpose whole-body controllers provide a reusable starting point; their original pretraining is outside this task-adaptation measurement. We apply the same boundary to related systems by separating task learning from the acquisition of their inherited controllers and priors.

SLMP reports approximately eight hours for combat-policy training, excluding its tracking and latent-prior stages (Tan et al., 2026). Its hardware description lists a server with two RTX 4090 GPUs without specifying allocation to each stage. RoboStriker reports a single RTX 4090 but no wall-clock duration in the checked paper or preview README (Yin et al., 2026; RoboStriker Authors, 2026). GGSD reports 70000 joint skill-learning and self-play updates, without a wall-clock duration or a separate comparable adaptation stage (Rho et al., 2026). The evidence supports minute-scale boxing adaptation from an available general-purpose controller. Differences in inherited skills, hardware, observations, and task objectives prevent a controlled speedup factor or a fastest-method claim.

\calmregular5.4 \calmregularBoxing behavior after short adaptation

Six frozen policies share the packaged robot, physical parameters, arena, and referee. The participants are HoloBoxing (7-min version), its long version, two component removals, RoboStriker, and GGSD run2 (ggsd-demo, ). External opponents retain released weights without destination fine-tuning. Each of ten rounds covers all fifteen unordered pairs, with randomized sides and recorded initial-state seeds. Every pair therefore plays ten bouts, and each participant plays fifty. Elo starts at 1500 with K=16K=16; the fixed evaluation budget is independent of intermediate ranks. Appendix D gives the scoring thresholds and rating equation.

HoloBoxing (7-min version) ranks second in the fixed six-policy league; the long version ranks first. Table 3 reports the complete outcomes, while Table 4 separates opponent groups. The primary version wins seven of ten bouts against GGSD and four of ten against RoboStriker. Its contact deficit against RoboStriker limits claims about offensive strength. The long version wins eight of ten bouts against the primary version. Contacts and falls remain necessary context: four primary-version wins contain no scored hand contact.

Table 4 separates external opponents from component controls.

\calmregular5.5 \calmregularRoles of initialization and the target representation

The 7-min version and its component removals use one seed, 128 environments, and identical 24-step rollouts. The primary HoloBoxing model provides the reference for the two component removals. All complete 32 standing updates and 128 final updates, totaling 491520 learner transitions per group. Matching applies to learner transitions; fitting costs differ when imitation is removed. HoloBoxing (7-min version) retains all upper-policy components, with newly fitted imitation initialization and a reused frozen latent prior. HoloBoxing w/o imitation initialization removes imitation parameter updates while preserving initial observation statistics and the same frozen prior. HoloBoxing w/o latent decoder replaces the 32-dimensional latent action and decoder with a direct 225-dimensional target policy through the same frozen lower controller. The 7-min version and direct-target variant each receive 20 imitation epochs from the identical measured training population. All three final stages use the same external frozen standing actor, with its exact original normalizer and no opponent refresh. The last scheduled checkpoint is selected before competitive evaluation.

The primary 7-min version combines a 6.25-minute new run with 0.79 minutes of previously recorded target-prior fitting. The variant without imitation also reuses that prior; the direct-target variant has no target prior. Time labels therefore include target-representation fitting while excluding the common pretrained lower controller. The long version uses separate RTX 5090 runs: 47 seconds for prior fitting, 19 for imitation, 247 for standing, and 969 for interaction. It uses 256 final updates against its own frozen warmup actor. The primary version and both component removals use RTX 4090 and 128 final updates. Their elapsed times are consequently not a matched-hardware scaling comparison. Before training, the direct-target policy’s exploration is calibrated against the latent policy using physical target perturbations, rather than equal numerical action noise. Both removals retain the 7-min version label to identify their reference configuration, rather than an identical measured duration. The scale is selected from three prespecified candidates without match rewards. Position and rotation perturbation magnitudes are comparable, while covariance and optimization geometry can still differ. Appendix C.4 reports the measured calibration values. In the same league, the 7-min version ranks above both component removals and produces more scored contacts. This is consistent with using imitation initialization and a structured target interface under the tested 128-update final-stage budget. The comparison does not isolate each component’s effect on convergence time. Removing the decoder also changes action dimension and exploration geometry, so its result concerns the complete action-interface choice.

\calmregular5.6 \calmregularChoosing a compact but executable representation

Select information before adding history.

Table 6 compares eight observation choices with the same frozen decoder and three seeds per condition. Current-state input with opponent information gives the lowest mean supervised validation loss, 16.9% below ten-frame history with opponent input. This supports the selected feedback information for imitation initialization; it does not independently demonstrate faster reinforcement learning.

Check execution as well as reconstruction.

The selected reconstruction and uncompressed targets each complete 80 of 81 predefined validation windows, failing the same source window. This supports retaining a compact representation without adding failures in that measured population. A later candidate reduces reconstruction loss but introduces an additional tracking failure and loses required frame coverage in its separate fixed comparison. It is therefore not promoted. Appendix C.2 specifies the populations, height gate, and coverage accounting.

Measured-frame labels are also harder to reconstruct than paired reference-frame targets with the same frozen representation. This motivates checking the target interface under actual robot feedback, alongside reference reconstruction. Appendix C gives the capacity, held-out, and paired-target diagnostics.

\calmregular6 \calmregularDiscussion

Why the recipe is simple.

HoloBoxing assigns motor execution, target structure, and task decisions to separate components. The pretrained controller supplies feedback-based movement execution, while the decoder turns compact actions into requests that controller can follow. Measured-state imitation connects robot observations to those requests before task rewards refine the planner. The same interfaces persist across stages, so task adaptation reuses the decoder and controller instead of rebuilding their capabilities.

Why short adaptation is possible.

The recipe confines task learning to the upper policy and its training objectives. A 32-dimensional action replaces direct prediction of 225 future-target coordinates, and supervised examples provide the initial feedback behavior. The recorded cost shows that representation fitting and initialization occupy a small part of the selected training path. Most recorded training time is spent on standing and interaction, after reusable execution and target structure are already available. This explains the allocation of work; it does not establish an isolated causal speedup for each design choice.

What the experiments show.

The seven-minute training path produces scored boxing interaction and ranks second in the evaluated pool. The 21.4-minute long version ranks first. With 128 final-stage updates, the 7-min version yields stronger league outcomes than either component removal. The representation studies also show why a low reconstruction loss alone is insufficient: the selected targets must remain physically executable. Together, the experiments assess how the recipe’s interfaces and initialization support the behavior obtained within its budget.

Limitations and future work.

The study uses a small motion corpus and one selected task-training seed. The reported time measures additional learning above an available general-purpose controller, excluding its pretraining, preparation, and search. The primary learner also reuses a task-specific standing opponent whose original training is excluded. This is a task-adaptation comparison; methods may inherit different motor capabilities and representations. Independent seeds and matched timing studies are needed to isolate component effects on learning speed. The direct-target control changes action dimension and exploration geometry along with removing the decoder. The league is not a fully controlled comparison: methods retain different state encodings, history, and auxiliary inputs. Our upper planner retains 78 observation features, but the frozen lower controller also consumes robot feedback. A smaller upper-policy input therefore does not establish a smaller information budget for the complete system. External policies also receive no destination fine-tuning. League outcomes consequently describe these checkpoint systems rather than establish method superiority. Our efficiency result is minute-scale additional training above reusable motor control; the available budgets do not establish a universally fastest method. Terminal wins also require contact and fall statistics because a knockout can follow an opponent’s unforced fall. Future work should broaden motion and reset coverage and test alternative lower controllers. The current experiments are simulation-only; real-robot boxing and transfer remain untested.

\calmregular7 \calmregularConclusion

HoloBoxing combines a pretrained whole-body controller, a compact target representation, measured-state imitation, and task reinforcement learning. Its simplicity comes from separating motor execution from task decisions and reusing the controller and decoder throughout task adaptation. The latent target interface reduces the planner’s action dimension, while imitation supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven interaction. The primary recipe accounts for about seven minutes of additional training above an available controller. A 21.4-minute long version improves league outcomes at greater training cost. Boxing experiments demonstrate scored interaction, and matched-budget controls examine the roles of initialization and target representation. The study supports this combined recipe under the measured conditions; it does not isolate each component’s contribution to training speed.

Appendix A Reproduction settings

The selected recipe uses Unitree G1 and the frozen HoloMotion v2 controller [Horizon Robotics, 2026]. Reference motions combine InterHuman [Liang et al., 2024] and released RoboStriker trajectories [RoboStriker Authors, 2026]. All frames, mirrored copies, participants, and overlapping windows from one original motion group stay in the same split. The prior uses 21148 training, 11074 validation, and 3246 test windows. Planner initialization uses 2568 measured training examples and 6448 validation examples from different motion groups. These counts describe a small-data experiment, rather than a prescribed competition corpus.

Prior fitting uses Adam, batch size 1024, and learning rate 10−310^{-3}. PPO uses five optimization epochs, four minibatches, adaptive learning-rate control initialized at 10−510^{-5}, discount 0.99, advantage parameter 0.95, and clipping threshold 0.2. Validation selects the reused prior; imitation uses 20 epochs with batch size 256 and learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. The last scheduled imitation and interaction checkpoints are used. The interaction stage collects 393216 learner transitions; standing adds 98304, totaling 491520. The primary version and both component removals use seed 43 and the same frozen external standing opponent, without refresh. The accounted seven minutes include previously recorded prior fitting and the complete new single-RTX-4090 process. Lower-controller pretraining, preparation, evaluation, and search are excluded. The long version instead uses 256 final updates and its own frozen warmup opponent.

Appendix B Objectives and target coordinates

Section 3 defines the execution chain and the representation and imitation objectives. This appendix specifies the coordinate alignment and detailed loss used with those interfaces. For five points and five future samples, three position and six orientation features give 225=5×5×(3+6)225=5\times 5\times(3+6) target coordinates.

Measured-state imitation.

The controller tracks source motions while collection records actual robot observations and future-target labels. Future reference states provide labels, rather than actor inputs. For measured pelvis pose (cm,Rm)(c^{m},R^{m}) and reference pose (cr,Rr)(c^{r},R^{r}), paired position targets satisfy

pm=(Rm)𝖳​(Rr​pr+cr+δt−cm).p^{m}=(R^{m})^{\mathsf{T}}(R^{r}p^{r}+c^{r}+\delta_{t}-c^{m}). (5)

The orientation encoding changes by (Rm)𝖳​Rr(R^{m})^{\mathsf{T}}R^{r}. The shared alignment translation averages horizontal displacement errors across the JJ participants:

δt=diag⁡(1,1,0)​1J​∑j=1J[(ct,jm−ct0,jm)−(ct,jr−ct0,jr)].\delta_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}[(c^{m}_{t,j}-c^{m}_{t_{0},j})-(c^{r}_{t,j}-c^{r}_{t_{0},j})]. (6)

Here, t0t_{0} is the collection-window reset. The same translation shifts all future points and participants, while orientations remain unchanged. The target loss in Equation 4 is

ℓtarget​(x^,x)=λpK​H​dp​‖(x^p−xp)⊘σp‖22+1−λpK​H​dr​‖(x^r−xr)⊘σr‖22.\ell_{\mathrm{target}}(\hat{x},x)=\frac{\lambda_{p}}{KHd_{p}}\|(\hat{x}^{p}-x^{p})\oslash\sigma_{p}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1-\lambda_{p}}{KHd_{r}}\|(\hat{x}^{r}-x^{r})\oslash\sigma_{r}\|_{2}^{2}. (7)

Training statistics use positive standard-deviation floors, and λp=0.5\lambda_{p}=0.5. Gradients update the planner while preserving decoder weights.

Exploration and likelihood.

PPO stores the raw Gaussian latent sample and its conditional log-probability before normalization. Its likelihood ratio therefore concerns the sampled action rather than the normalized direction. Standing warmup and task refinement use initial exploration scales 0.1 and 0.2, with temporal correlation 0.9.

Appendix C Representation checks and component controls

\calmregularC.1 \calmregularObservation and reconstruction studies

Table 6 in the main text reports the observation study. The remaining studies examine decoder capacity and target coverage.

The capacity study also uses three seeds per architecture.

\calmregularC.2 \calmregularPhysical tracking and held-out coverage

The selected reconstruction and uncompressed targets each complete 80 of 81 validation windows, failing the same source window. These windows cover six files from four original motion groups and 11014 fixed role-frames. Each window lasts at most two seconds, following up to ten warmup frames. Failure means pelvis or torso height below 0.30 m above the floor; source-reference height is retained for interpretation. Windows from one motion are correlated observations. A later candidate reduces validation loss from 0.045326 to 0.044545 but adds one tracking failure and misses 16 fixed comparison frames. The accepted decoder therefore remains selected.

Held-out reconstruction is evaluated after selection, without reselecting the decoder.

One seated-retreat InterHuman test clip contributes 97.7% of that source’s test reconstruction loss. Its two execution windows start below the upright height gate, for both original and reconstructed targets. This gate cannot establish whether reconstruction worsens execution of the intended seated motion. The result limits claims about representation coverage beyond upright behavior.

\calmregularC.3 \calmregularReference-to-measured target transfer

Paired source and measured labels use identical source frames and participants, with all representation weights and statistics fixed. The comparison includes both the coordinate change and alignment translation defined above.

Latent-only fitting uses 128 evenly spaced examples per measured validation group, totaling 256 examples. Only latent codes are optimized, with 100 Adam steps at learning rate 0.03. The residual is an attained local-fit error, rather than a decoder expressiveness bound or initialized-planner result.

\calmregularC.4 \calmregularAdditional controls

Direct-target exploration is calibrated using three prespecified physical-noise candidates without match rewards. At the final-stage setting, latent and direct-target policies induce position perturbations of 18.26 and 18.34 cm root-mean-square. Their rotation perturbations are 0.713 and 0.701 radians. Comparable magnitudes do not establish identical covariance or optimization geometry.

Appendix D League rules and opponent interfaces

All six current participants share the packaged robot, actuator parameters, arena, simulator, and contact referee. Only the current ten-round, 150-bout league contributes to the reported ranking.

Scoring and ratings.

Legal hand contacts against the opponent’s head or torso, including pelvis targets, accumulate normal impulse at each 5 ms physics step. A 5 N⋅\cdots threshold within 20 ms scores one point, consumes that impulse, and starts a 200 ms cooldown for that hand. Ground contacts and foot strikes do not score. Pelvis or torso height below 0.30 m above the ring starts a fall timer. A continuous three-second fall confirms a knockout, awards the opponent 1000 points, and ends the bout. Earlier observed falls determine knockout precedence; simultaneous confirmed falls produce a draw even when hit scores differ. Otherwise, the 60-second timeout uses score, with equal scores producing a draw.

Each round covers all fifteen unordered pairs once, with randomized sides and recorded initial-state perturbations and sampling seeds. Every participant starts at 1500 Elo, with pre-match ratings used for both updates:

EA=(1+10(RB−RA)/400)−1,ΔA=round⁡(16​(SA−EA)).E_{A}=(1+10^{(R_{B}-R_{A})/400})^{-1},\qquad\Delta_{A}=\operatorname{round}(16(S_{A}-E_{A})). (8)

Here, SA∈{0,12,1}S_{A}\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{2},1\}; A gains ΔA\Delta_{A} and B loses the same amount. Score margins and knockout bonuses do not multiply Elo updates. Execution faults stop dispatch without replacement seeds, forfeits, or imputed outcomes. The fixed ten-round budget is independent of intermediate ranks.

The two external opponents use the released RoboStriker G1 Stage-3 and GGSD run2 checkpoints. Both retain source-trained weights and receive no destination fine-tuning.

Replay and measurement limits.

Recorded robot states, actions, contacts, and referee events support replay without rerunning policies or physics. A current dispatch check matches all 3000 non-timing frames across two RTX 4090 GPUs for one unchanged long-version–RoboStriker case. This bounded check does not establish universal hardware determinism, identical retraining, or real-robot behavior.

\calmregularD.1 \calmregularInference timing

A fixed-pose RTX 4090 microbenchmark of the long version includes observation construction, planner, decoder, frozen controller, recurrent-state updates, and target conversion. It excludes physics and output sanitation, and synchronizes the GPU around every timed interval. After ten warmup iterations, 100 measured iterations average 3.182 ms, with empirical 99th percentile 3.373 ms. The environment uses Warp 1.11.0, ONNX Runtime 1.22.0, CUDA 12.8.90, and driver 580.95.05. These fixed-pose samples do not establish full-match or hard real-time latency.

Appendix E Recorded boxing examples

Figure E.1 shows recorded bouts from the primary 7-min version. The examples include a win against GGSD and a loss against RoboStriker, illustrating approach and scored exchanges in both directions. Frames are reconstructed from saved robot poses without policy inference or physics stepping. The selection illustrates behavior; it is not an estimate of win rate.
